criteria.remark: Two images, one on each of two pages, carry no alternative text: the main hero graphic on the home page and the profile picture in the account area. A screen reader has nothing to announce in their place, so whatever these images convey is unavailable to someone who cannot see them.

Sixteen in-page links across five pages point to a destination that does not exist: pressing Enter on them, including the "skip" link in each page header aimed at #main-content, leaves focus where it was, because no element on the page carries that id or name. What was measured is only the link and its target; a person has to decide whether another mechanism bypasses the same blocks — a heading, a landmark or a collapsible block. Several of the flagged links are case-number controls inside a data table rather than bypass mechanisms. skip-link-works could not look on 1 of 37 scans (the path is replayed once for each rule, and this rule needed its end loaded again); what it would have found is not shown.

Eighteen links across six pages have no text a screen reader can announce. Each is an icon-only link: a small graphic marked as decorative sits inside the link, with no visible text, label or title alongside it. The three social media links repeated across pages, which lead to outside benefits pages, are examples. Someone using a screen reader reaches these links in the tab order and hears nothing that identifies where they lead.

On the application form, one field — the date of birth box — has more than one label element attached to it. What was measured is the presence of those labels, not their wording; the text of each was not captured, so whether the first label alone carries everything needed, such as the expected date format held in the hint, is undetermined. A person has to decide this point: "Multiple label elements is not widely supported in assistive technologies. Ensure the first label contains all necessary information."

rationales: The check names two labels, label[for="dob"] and .hint-label, but the payload carries no text for either. Whether the first label alone conveys everything (e.g. the expected date format in the hint) cannot be determined from the markup given.

criteria.remark: The VPAT® template answers this criterion itself: the September 2023 errata make it always satisfied under WCAG 2.0 and 2.1, and WCAG 2.2 removed it as obsolete. MANTA did not evaluate it.

Twenty elements across six pages give assistive technology no name to report. Most are icon-only links whose only content is a graphic marked as decorative, including the social media links repeated across pages; the rest are form controls with nothing attached to name them, such as the Social Security number box on the application form. A screen reader user meets these in the tab order and is told only that a link or a field is there, not what it is for.

On three pages the same "Pending" status badge is set in amber text on white, measuring 2.27 to 1 against its background, where 4.5 to 1 is the threshold for text that size, so the status is hard to read for people with low vision. One further piece of text, in an upload dialog shown over a dimmed backdrop, could not be measured because the colour behind it was undetermined; a person has to judge that one against the page as it renders.

Eight form controls across two pages — the first name, last name, date of birth and Social Security number boxes and the household size dropdown on the application form among them — show a focus outline in pale amber measuring 1.66 to 1 against the white surface behind it, where 3 to 1 is the threshold for such an indicator. That measurement is settled; the outline's thickness and any other change the controls make when focused were not captured, so a person has to decide whether another visual cue identifies the focus.
